title: Tamar. Rahab. Ruth. Bathsheba. Why Are These Women Named Before Jesus Is Born?
paragraphs: Tamar. Rahab. Ruth. Bathsheba. Why Are These Women Named Before Jesus Is Born?

Before Matthew tells us about the virgin, the manger, the wise men, or the Child called Jesus, he makes us walk through a family history filled with sexual scandal, outsiders, grief, shattered reputations, abuse of power, and astonishing grace. And he does it for a reason.
Most people hurry through genealogies.
Abraham begot Isaac. Isaac begot Jacob. Jacob begot Judah.
Names.
More names.
More names.
We want Bethlehem. We want angels. We want the star. We want Mary holding the newborn Christ.
But Matthew will not let us get to the manger that quickly.
Before he shows us Jesus, he opens the family records.
And hidden among generations of fathers and sons, four references suddenly interrupt the rhythm.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
And “the wife of Uriah”—Bathsheba.
Then comes Mary.
If you have ever wondered whether the parts of your story that embarrass you have permanently disqualified you from being used by God, do not rush past these women.
Stay here.
Because before Matthew announces the birth of the Savior, he deliberately reminds us what kind of world the Savior came to save.
Matthew begins:
“Βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ…”
Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou.
“The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ…” — Matthew 1:1.
Then the rhythm begins.
Father.
Son.
Father.
Son.
Generation after generation.
Until Matthew writes that Judah fathered Perez and Zerah “ἐκ τῆς Θάμαρ”—ek tēs Thamar, “by Tamar.”
Later: Boaz “ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ”—by Rahab.
Then Obed “ἐκ τῆς Ῥούθ”—by Ruth.
Then Solomon “ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου”—literally, by “the [woman] of Uriah.”
Matthew does not even call Bathsheba by name there.
He calls attention to Uriah.
And suddenly this genealogy is not merely a list.
It is a testimony.
Not because these women were the only sinners in Jesus’ genealogy. Far from it. The men surrounding them were sinners too, sometimes spectacularly so.
And not because Matthew is teaching that women themselves were somehow scandalous intrusions into an otherwise respectable family line.
No.
The shock is much deeper.
God did not sanitize the human history into which His Son entered.
Jesus stepped directly into it.
Tamar’s story is uncomfortable enough that many Christians have probably never heard a sermon about it.
Genesis 38 introduces us to a family collapsing under sin.

Tamar married Judah’s son Er. Er died under divine judgment. According to the family obligation described in the narrative, Judah’s next son, Onan, was expected to preserve his dead brother’s line through Tamar. Instead, he exploited the situation while deliberately refusing the responsibility attached to it. He also died under judgment.
Judah then promised Tamar his younger son Shelah when the boy grew older.
But Judah did not keep his word.
Tamar waited.
And waited.
And eventually realized she had been abandoned in a vulnerable position.
What happened next is disturbing and complicated. Tamar disguised herself, Judah mistook her for a prostitute, and Judah slept with his own daughter-in-law without realizing who she was.
She became pregnant.
When Judah later heard that Tamar was pregnant, his response was terrifyingly hypocritical.
He wanted her punished.
Until Tamar produced the evidence showing who the father was.
And Judah finally confessed:
“צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי”
Tzadeqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Not “Tamar never sinned.”
Not “everything Tamar did should be imitated.”
Judah is acknowledging that, in the situation narrated, Tamar had been more in the right than he was because he had failed to give her Shelah as promised.
The scandal exposed something Judah would rather have kept hidden.
His own failure.
And from that broken chapter came Perez.
And through Perez eventually came David.
And through David eventually came Jesus.
Matthew refuses to erase Tamar from the record.
Her name remains.
Maybe that matters to someone reading this who has spent years believing that the worst chapter of your life became the title of your entire story.
Maybe people remember you by what happened.
Maybe they know the divorce.
The addiction.
The pregnancy.
The affair.
The betrayal.
The arrest.
The collapse.
The years you ran from God.
Maybe your own memory keeps dragging you back into rooms Jesus has already called you to leave.
Hear this carefully: grace does not mean sin never mattered.
The cross proves sin mattered so much that Christ had to die.
Grace means sin does not get the final word over everyone who comes to Christ.
Then Matthew writes another name.
Rahab.
If this is the Rahab of Joshua—as the longstanding Christian identification understands her—her résumé does not begin in a synagogue.
It begins in Jericho.
And Scripture identifies Rahab as a prostitute.
Not metaphorically.
Not because Christians later tried to make her past sound dramatic.
Hebrews still calls her that when celebrating her faith, and James likewise points to her actions in receiving and protecting the messengers.
Think about that.
God did not need Scripture to lie about Rahab’s past in order to honor what His grace produced in her.
That should free somebody.
We often think redemption requires pretending.
Pretending the addiction never happened.
Pretending the marriage was never broken.
Pretending we were never sexually immoral.
Pretending we never doubted.
Pretending we never became cold toward God.
Pretending our family was healthier than it really was.
The Bible does something much more powerful.
It tells the truth.
And then it shows what God can do with people whose truth is ugly.
Rahab had heard what Israel’s God had done.
And somewhere inside a woman surrounded by a condemned city, faith awakened.
She told the Israelite spies that the LORD their God was God in heaven above and on earth beneath.
Then she acted on what she believed.
Hebrews later summarizes it with two astonishing words:
“Πίστει Ῥαὰβ…”
Pistei Rhaab.
“By faith Rahab…”
By faith.
The prostitute became a woman remembered for faith.
Do not miss that.
Scripture remembers where she came from without imprisoning her there.
Her past remains part of her testimony.
It does not remain the master of her identity.
That is what Jesus does.
The Gospel is not God pretending you were always clean.
The Gospel is God cleansing people who cannot cleanse themselves.
It is not God announcing that rebellion was harmless.
It is God announcing that the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
There is a difference.
Maybe you have been trying to become worthy enough to come home.
You keep telling yourself, “After I fix this…”
“After I stop struggling…”
“After I become consistent…”
“After I get myself together…”
Then I will come back to God.
But if sinners could repair themselves before approaching God, we would not need a Savior.
Christ did not come as a trophy for people who successfully rescued themselves.
He came to seek and save the lost.
Rahab did not climb out of Jericho and eventually become worthy of mercy.
Mercy found her while Jericho was still Jericho.
Then comes Ruth.
Her story feels gentler, but underneath its tenderness is enormous pain.
Ruth is a widow.
Naomi is a widow.
The future looks empty.
And Ruth is a Moabite woman entering Israel.
Yet Ruth makes one of Scripture’s most breathtaking declarations of loyalty.
The Hebrew includes:
“עַמֵּךְ עַמִּי וֵאלֹהַיִךְ אֱלֹהָי”
‘Amekh ‘ammi, ve’Elohayikh Elohai.
“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.”
Those are not merely romantic words about human loyalty.
Ruth is binding her future to Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God.
She walks toward Bethlehem with a grieving woman who believes she has come home empty.
Think about the irony.
Naomi says she came home empty.
But walking beside her is Ruth.
And inside Ruth’s future is Obed.
Inside Obed’s future is Jesse.
Inside Jesse’s future is David.
And inside David’s royal line, according to the promise of God, is the coming Messiah.
Naomi thought she was looking at emptiness.
God was writing genealogy.
Maybe that is where this article finds you.
You have been calling this season empty.
Empty bank account.
Empty bedroom.
Empty chair.
Empty marriage.
Empty prayers.
Empty plans.
Empty heart.
You prayed and nothing happened the way you expected.
You lost someone.
Someone left.
Something died that you were sure God would preserve.
And now you are standing in the ruins trying to understand how a good God could possibly write anything beautiful from this.
Ruth whispers across the centuries:
You cannot always tell what God is doing by looking at what you have lost.
Sometimes providence looks like an ordinary road back to Bethlehem.
Sometimes redemption enters wearing work clothes and gleaning grain from the edges of somebody else’s field.
Sometimes the chapter that feels like an ending is carrying a beginning you cannot yet see.
Then comes the most haunting reference of all.
Matthew does not say “Bathsheba.”
He writes of “the wife of Uriah.”
That wording makes the reader remember.
Uriah.
The faithful soldier.
The husband David betrayed.

Second Samuel does not soften David’s actions. David saw Bathsheba, inquired about her, sent messengers, and had her brought to him. After she became pregnant, David attempted to conceal what he had done. Eventually he arranged for Uriah to be placed where he would be killed in battle.
Then David took Bathsheba as his wife.
For a moment, the king may have believed the story had been buried.
But God sent Nathan.
That matters.
Because biblical grace is never permission to protect powerful people from truth.
The Bible does not rewrite David’s evil into romance.
It exposes it.
And Matthew, generations later, refuses to let the royal genealogy become propaganda.
“The wife of Uriah.”
Four words that keep the wound visible.
Four words reminding every king that God remembers the person power would prefer to erase.
And yet…
Solomon came through Bathsheba.
The royal line continued.
Not because David’s sin was acceptable.
Not because Uriah’s death was insignificant.
Not because consequences disappeared.
But because human evil could not cancel God’s redemptive purpose.
That is one of the hardest truths of grace.
God can redeem what He never approved.
Read that again.
God can redeem what He never approved.
He can bring beauty out of a situation without calling the evil beautiful.
He can forgive sin without redefining sin.
He can restore sinners without pretending nobody was wounded.
He can write redemption after devastation without asking us to call devastation good.
That is why Christianity is not positive thinking.
It is resurrection.
Positive thinking tells the tomb to look less dark.
Jesus walks into death and comes out alive.
And now we begin to understand why these women appear before the birth of Christ.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
The wife of Uriah.
Different women.
Different wounds.
Different circumstances.
Different moral complexities.
We should not flatten their stories into one category.
Tamar was not Rahab.
Ruth was not Bathsheba.
Bathsheba should not be blamed for David’s abuse of royal power.
Ruth’s loyalty should not be treated as scandal merely because she was a Moabite.
Their stories deserve to be heard as Scripture actually tells them.
But Matthew places their memories into the genealogy leading toward Jesus.
And then comes another woman.
Mary.
And suddenly the pattern reaches its climax.
Matthew has been saying “begot… begot… begot…”
Until Jesus.
The wording changes.
Joseph is identified as the husband of Mary, “of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.”
Jesus is not presented as Joseph’s biological son.
Matthew is preparing us for the virgin conception he immediately explains.
The genealogy reaches Jesus Christ, but Jesus enters the story uniquely.
The Savior comes into the human family while remaining the promised Christ.
He inherits a real human history.
A history containing kings and prostitutes, patriarchs and outsiders, faithful people and catastrophic sinners.
He does not stand at a safe distance from our wreckage.
He enters the human story.
And eventually He carries human sin to a Roman cross.
This is where genealogy becomes Gospel.
Because maybe Tamar is not the person in this story you recognize.
Maybe Judah is.
Maybe you were the hypocrite.
Maybe Rahab is not the person you recognize.
Maybe you are the person who lived for years in rebellion while knowing somewhere inside that God was real.
Maybe Ruth is you.
Still faithful.
Still walking.
Still grieving.
Still wondering why obedience has become so expensive.
Maybe you recognize David.
And that terrifies you.
Because you did something that wounded somebody.
You covered it.
You justified it.
You blamed circumstances.
You hoped time would bury it.
But the Holy Spirit keeps bringing you back to the truth.
Then do not run from conviction.
Run with it to Christ.
Repentance is not God destroying your hope.
Repentance is God refusing to let the thing destroying you remain hidden.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Blood-bought forgiveness.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because humanity needed motivational advice.
He died because we needed atonement.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed mercy.
We needed a righteousness we could never manufacture for ourselves.
The genealogy points toward a Child.
The Child grows toward a cross.
And the cross opens an empty tomb.
That is the Gospel.
Your sin is more serious than the world tells you.
And the grace of Jesus Christ is more powerful than your shame tells you.
You cannot save yourself.
But Christ actually saves sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People who have been wounded.
People who have wounded others.
People whose families are complicated.
People who wish they could tear pages out of their own biographies.
Jesus does not ask you to edit your history before coming to Him.
He asks you to repent and believe.
Bring Him the truth.
The real truth.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The sexual sin.
The pride.
The secret messages.
The resentment.
The hypocrisy.
The unbelief.
The hidden browser history.
The anger toward God.
The years you wasted.
The thing nobody knows.
Bring it into the light.
Not because confession earns salvation.
Jesus earns salvation.
But the person who comes to Christ no longer has to build a home inside the darkness.
There is a dangerous version of Christianity that teaches people how to look redeemed without actually surrendering.
Smile.
Post a verse.
Attend church.
Say “God is good.”
Keep the secret locked downstairs.
Jesus wants deeper than your image.
He wants you.
And maybe that is why this genealogy feels so strangely comforting.
The Bible is not embarrassed by broken people.
It simply refuses to leave brokenness unchallenged and unredeemed.
God's grace does not airbrush Scripture's families.
It invades them.
Tamar’s chapter was not deleted.
Rahab’s former life was not rewritten.
Ruth’s foreignness was not concealed.
Uriah’s name was not erased to protect David’s reputation.
And still…
Jesus came.
That may be the three-word sermon somebody desperately needs tonight.
Jesus still came.
After Abraham’s failures.
After Jacob’s deception.
After Judah’s hypocrisy.
After Tamar.
After Rahab.
After Ruth’s grief.
After David and Bathsheba.
After murder.
After idolatry.
After divided kingdoms.
After exile.
After generations of waiting.
Jesus still came.
And if you think your family is too dysfunctional for God to touch, look at His genealogy.
If you think your history is too dirty for grace, look toward His cross.
If you think you wandered too far, look at Rahab.
If grief convinced you nothing remains, remember Ruth walking into Bethlehem.
If hidden sin is eating you alive, remember David standing before Nathan.
If somebody else’s sin has become part of your story, remember that Scripture can tell the truth about the wound without making the wound your final identity.
And if shame keeps whispering, “People like you do not belong near Jesus,” open Matthew 1.
Read the names again.
Then keep reading until you reach the name above every name.
Jesus.
Ἰησοῦς.
The name Matthew connects with the announcement that He will save His people from their sins.
Not merely inspire them.
Not merely improve their reputation.
Save them.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
But understand what that means.
Grace does not mean scandal becomes sacred.
Grace means Jesus is greater than the scandal.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace turns people from darkness toward the Light.
Grace does not tell sinners to remain exactly as they are.
Grace meets us where we are, forgives us through Christ, and begins transforming us into people who increasingly look like Him.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess honestly.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy purchased at the cross.
You do not have to publish the details.
God already knows them.
Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed person finally believes there is still a road home.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page either.
Not as a performance.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with heaven.
There may come a night when shame tries to rename you.
Come back and read the genealogy again.
Because the first chapter of Matthew destroys that illusion.
Christianity is for sinners because Christ came to save sinners.
Come to Jesus.
A ministry cannot cleanse you.
A book cannot justify you.
A shirt cannot redeem you.
A church cannot die in your place.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Support ministry if the Lord leads you.
Share truth because you love people.
Give because you love God.
But never confuse supporting the messenger with receiving the Message.
The Gospel is Jesus Christ crucified for sinners and risen from the dead.

And the same Savior whose genealogy carried memories of Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah is still gathering people with histories nobody would have chosen and writing testimonies nobody could have imagined.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“How could God ever use someone with a story like mine?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What might Jesus write next if I finally surrender the pen?”
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
Bathsheba.
And then…
Jesus.
The genealogy was never telling you that sin does not matter.
It was preparing you to meet the One powerful enough to redeem sinners.
And remember this when shame comes knocking again:
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you wish had never been written; He went to the cross so it would not have to be the final chapter.
